unit_title: Unit I: Introduction and OS Structures

topics.title: Definition & Functions of an Operating System
topics.content_html:
Operating System (OS): System software that acts as an intermediary between user applications and the computer hardware.

  • Functions: Process Management, Memory Management, Storage Management, I/O Management, Security & Protection.
Example: Memory Management (allocating RAM to Chrome), Process Management (CPU scheduling), I/O (handling printers).

topics.title: Modes of Operation & Protection
topics.content_html:
Dual-Mode Operation: OS uses a Mode Bit to protect itself and other system components.

  • User Mode (Bit=1): Executing user applications. Restricted access.
  • Kernel Mode (Bit=0): Executing OS code. Full access to hardware.

Timer Interrupts: Prevents user programs from freezing the system (e.g. infinite loops). When a timer interrupt occurs, mode bit changes to 0, returning control to OS.

Exam Trap: User programs cannot directly access hardware like printers; a system call must be invoked to enter kernel mode.

topics.title: I/O & Memory Access (DMA vs Programmed I/O)
topics.content_html:
• Programmed I/O: CPU waits for I/O device. High CPU involvement, low efficiency.
  • Interrupt-Driven I/O: CPU does other work until I/O interrupts. More efficient.
  • Direct Memory Access (DMA): Device controller transfers data directly to/from memory without CPU intervention. Most efficient for bulk data.

topics.title: Interrupts: Hardware vs Software
topics.content_html:
• Hardware Interrupts: Triggered by hardware devices (e.g., timer, keyboard).
  • Software Interrupts (Traps): Triggered by software executing a system call or encountering an error (divide by zero).

topics.title: Types of Operating Systems
topics.content_html:
• Batch OS: Groups similar jobs. Limitation: No user interaction, CPU idle during I/O.
  • Multiprogramming: Keeps multiple jobs in memory to maximize CPU utilization.
  • Time-Sharing: Extends multiprogramming; gives each user a small time slice (fair share, interactive).
  • Real-Time OS: Strict deadlines (e.g., hospital life-support).

topics.title: System Calls
topics.content_html:
System Calls: Interface between a running program and the OS kernel.

  • Categories: Process Control (fork), File Management (read/write), Device Management (ioctl), Information Maintenance (gettimeofday), Communications (pipe).
Trace of 'Print': User clicks Print -> User program makes System Call -> Switch to Kernel Mode -> OS device driver communicates with Device Controller -> Controller performs I/O -> Interrupt sent back -> OS handles interrupt -> Return to User Mode.

topics.title: System Architectures
topics.content_html:
• Single-Processor: One CPU.
  • Multiprocessor: Multiple CPUs, tight coupling, higher reliability/throughput.
  • Clustered: Multiple separate machines working together. Best for high availability (survives complete machine failure).

topics.title: OS Structures
topics.content_html:
• Simple/Monolithic: Fast (no overhead), but hard to maintain. A bug in one driver crashes the whole kernel.
  • Layered: Easy to debug, but strict layers cause performance overhead.
  • Microkernel: Moves non-essential services to user space. High reliability, but slower due to message passing.
  • Module-Based (Hybrid): Dynamically loadable modules (e.g., Linux). Balances monolithic performance with microkernel modularity. Solves monolithic crash issues.

topics.title: Processes, Programs & Process Control Block
topics.content_html:
Program: Passive entity on disk. Process: Active entity running in memory.

Process Control Block (PCB): Data structure maintaining process state.

  • Attributes: Process State, Program Counter, CPU Registers, CPU Scheduling Info.

topics.title: Context Switching
topics.content_html: Context Switching: Saving the state of the old process and loading the saved state for a new process. Occurs on: Timer interrupts, I/O requests, higher-priority arrivals.

topics.title: Threads & Multithreading
topics.content_html:
• User Threads: Managed by user-level library. Fast, but if one thread blocks, the entire process blocks (because CPU only sees kernel threads).
  • Kernel Threads: Managed by OS. Slower, but supports true concurrency on multiprocessors.
Example: Word spell check (user thread) must be mapped/linked to a kernel thread to run on the CPU. A browser tab freezing doesn't affect others because tabs run on separate kernel threads/processes.

topics.title: Process Life Cycle & States
topics.content_html:
States:

  • New: Being created.
  • Ready: Waiting for CPU.
  • Running: Executing instructions.
  • Waiting (Blocked): Waiting for an event (e.g., I/O).
  • Terminated: Finished execution.
Exam Trap: A process moves to Waiting when doing I/O, but to Ready when interrupted by a timer.

topics.title: Schedulers & Queues
topics.content_html:
• Long-Term: Selects from disk to memory (controls degree of multiprogramming).
  • Short-Term: Selects from Ready Queue to allocate CPU. (Very frequent)
  • Medium-Term: Swaps processes in/out of memory temporarily (e.g. while waiting for I/O).

Ready Queue: Processes waiting for CPU. Waiting Queue: Processes waiting for I/O completion.

topics.title: CPU Scheduling Criteria
topics.content_html:
• Utilization: Keep CPU as busy as possible.
  • Throughput: Processes completed per time unit.
  • Turnaround Time (TAT): Completion Time - Arrival Time.
  • Waiting Time (WT): Turnaround Time - Burst Time.
  • Response Time (RT): Time from submission to first response (First Start - Arrival Time).

topics.title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms
topics.content_html:
• Preemptive vs Non-Preemptive: Preemptive (RR, SRTF) can interrupt a running process. Non-preemptive (FCFS, basic SJF) cannot.
  • FCFS: Simple, but suffers from Convoy Effect. Best for Batch.
  • SJF/SRTF: Optimal average waiting time, but predicting burst time is hard.
  • Round Robin (RR): Time quantum-based. Excellent for interactive Time-Sharing systems.
  • Priority: Highest priority runs first. Limitation: Starvation (e.g. process skipped forever). Solution: Aging.

topics.title: Concurrency & Atomic Operations
topics.content_html:
Concurrency: Multiple tasks making progress simultaneously. Example: Downloading a file while browsing.

Atomic Operation: An indivisible operation that completes entirely without interruption. High-level statements like counter++ are NOT atomic (they involve LOAD, ADD, STORE steps at machine level).

topics.title: Process Communication (IPC)
topics.content_html:
• Independent: Cannot affect others. Cooperating: Can affect others (e.g. Web browser and download manager).
  • Shared Memory: Fast, no OS involvement after setup. Needs synchronization.
  • Message Passing: Handled by OS, slower (data copying), no conflicts.

topics.title: Critical Section Problem
topics.content_html:
Critical Section: Part of code where shared resources are accessed. Divided into Entry, Critical, Exit, and Remainder sections.

  • Mutual Exclusion: Only one process in critical section.
  • Progress: If no one is in CS, someone can enter.
  • Bounded Waiting: A process won't wait forever.

topics.title: Hardware & Software Synchronization
topics.content_html:
• Peterson's Solution: Software approach using flag[] and turn. Satisfies all three requirements.
  • Test-and-Set Lock: Hardware instruction. Atomic. Can cause starvation (violates Bounded Waiting) if a process repeatedly re-acquires the lock while another waits indefinitely.

topics.title: Semaphores & Monitors
topics.content_html:
Semaphore: Integer variable accessed via atomic wait() and signal().

  • Counting: Unrestricted domain (e.g., tracking empty slots in a buffer).
  • Binary: 0 or 1 (acts as a mutex lock).

Disadvantages: Busy waiting, risk of deadlock.

Monitors: High-level abstraction. Easier to use than semaphores, prevents timing errors.

topics.title: Classical Problems of Synchronization
topics.content_html:
• Bounded Buffer (Producer-Consumer): Uses mutex, empty (tracks empty slots), and full (tracks filled slots). Race condition occurs if counter++ and counter-- interleave.
  • Readers-Writers: Hospital db scenario. Uses mutex, wrt, readcount. Writers have exclusive access, readers can share.
  • Dining Philosophers: Deadlock happens if all pick up left fork simultaneously. Solutions: Limit to 4 philosophers, pick up both or none, asymmetric picking.
